title: Role of the state in the macroeconomy

stages.name: Role of the state in the macroeconomy
stages.title: Role of the state in the macroeconomy
stages.sub: After this, you can explain monetary, exchange rate, supply-side and direct control policies, and why governments chase competitiveness.

steps.q: Inflation is too high. A committee decides to raise the cost of borrowing money across the whole economy. Which kind of body has the power to do this, rather than a random shop or firm?
steps.right: The one body that sets rates for the whole economy
steps.wrong: Any large private bank that lends money
steps.hint: Who sets the base rate that all other banks follow?

steps.q: The central bank raises interest rates and also controls how much money is created in the economy. What kind of policy is this, aimed at borrowing and the amount of money circulating?
steps.right: A policy using interest rates and the money supply
steps.wrong: A policy using government tax rates and spending
steps.hint: Think about what tool was actually changed: the price of borrowing, not taxes or spending.

steps.q: Instead of changing interest rates directly, the authorities buy or sell their own currency on the foreign exchange market to move its value. What are they now trying to manage?
steps.right: The value of the currency against others
steps.wrong: The amount of money circulating at home
steps.hint: Buying and selling currency changes its price against other currencies, not the domestic money supply.

steps.q: A government spends on training schemes and cuts red tape for new firms, hoping the economy can produce more in the long run without extra demand. Is this aimed at how much is spent, or at how much the economy is capable of producing?
steps.right: How much the economy is capable of producing
steps.wrong: How much people and firms spend
steps.hint: Training and cutting red tape change firms' ability to produce, not spending on goods.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Instead of training schemes, a government simply bans a certain type of pollution, sets a legal minimum wage, or fixes a maximum price by law. Is it changing incentives, or ordering a specific outcome?
steps.right: Ordering a specific outcome by law
steps.wrong: Changing incentives so firms choose it
steps.hint: A ban or a legal limit does not persuade anyone, it forces the outcome directly.

steps.q: A country's firms already sell more cheaply and to a higher standard than foreign rivals. A weaker currency would make its exports even cheaper abroad too. Why might a government want this: to sell more abroad, or simply to please foreign buyers?
steps.right: To sell more abroad and support jobs at home
steps.wrong: Simply to keep foreign buyers happy
steps.hint: Think about what higher export sales do for a country's own output and jobs.
